text: The single rule that matters most in this lesson: never put an API key, a database password, or any other credential into a prompt or system prompt. It feels convenient to just give the model the key so it can call an API directly, and it's exactly the wrong move, for reasons specific to how these systems actually work.

A context window isn't a private scratchpad. It can be logged for debugging, included in an observability trace, summarized into memory for a later turn, or read back out by an attacker who convinces the model to repeat part of its own context — the default assumption from Chapter 2 is that prompt-injection exposure exists. A secret that enters the prompt has to be treated as already leaked, whether or not you can point to the exact moment it happened.

The fix is keeping the model's reasoning path and the application's credential path genuinely separate, connected only at the moment a tool executes. The model decides that a tool should be called and with what arguments — look up order 4471, send a forty-dollar refund — but it never holds, sees, or needs the credential that actually performs the action. That's the orchestration layer's job, and it keeps real credentials out of anything fed back into the model's context, including the tool's own result.

This is exactly where managed identity and workload identity federation from Course 9 pay off specifically for AI applications. Every service-to-service call an orchestration layer makes on a tool's behalf is a candidate for an identity tied to the compute resource itself, with the cloud platform issuing short-lived tokens behind the scenes. There's no long-lived key to leak through a log, a config file, or a container image, because there's no long-lived key stored anywhere at all.

Managed identity doesn't remove every secret — a third-party API that only accepts a static key, or a legacy system with no identity federation, still needs one somewhere. For what's left, use a dedicated secrets vault rather than an environment variable or a file in source control, so access stays logged and rotation doesn't require a code change. And scan any data headed into training, fine-tuning, or a RAG index for embedded secrets first, because a credential baked into that data can resurface later through ordinary model output.

That closes Chapter 6: access control pushed into the retrieval query, API security tuned for cost and generated output, tool access scoped to a narrow blast radius, and credentials kept out of the model's reach entirely. Chapter 7 moves from architecture to process — red-teaming an AI application, building an AI-specific threat model, and the governance frameworks shaping where this is all heading.
